title: Songs Everyone Knew
subtitle: One parodist, and twelve years of borrowed hits
intro: A parody only works if you already know the song underneath it. Follow "Weird Al" Yankovic through six connections and twelve years of hits he borrowed, in the order they happened, and you get a map of which songs were big enough for everyone to know from 1984 to 1996. They also show his method of asking permission first, and the one time the two sides told the story differently.

steps.framing: Start with the breakthrough. 'Eat It' copied the music of Michael Jackson's 'Beat It' as closely as a different band could, with new words, and Jackson was asked first and said yes. It became Yankovic's first big hit in America. Jackson's approval, and his later refusal of a second parody, are both on this stop.

Copying a record that closely takes skill, and the joke depends on the copy being exact. Rick Derringer, a rock guitarist who is credited as producer on every Yankovic album from 1983 to 1992, played the 'Beat It' guitar solo again himself instead of lifting it from Jackson's record.

A year later it was Madonna's turn. 'Like a Surgeon' kept the music of 'Like a Virgin' and swapped the words for a joke about a nervous surgeon, and Madonna was fine with it: a second chart hit in two years, and an easy approval. Compare it with the last stop, where the permission story does not line up.

Not every borrowing is a parody. In a polka medley, his second regular form, Yankovic plays twelve Rolling Stones songs one after another as a fast accordion polka, using a whole catalogue as raw melody, and you can still recognise every tune. It reaches back to songs from 1965, so what everyone knew was not only what was in the charts that year.

By 1992 the song everyone knew was Nirvana's 'Smells Like Teen Spirit'. 'Smells Like Nirvana' copies its music and jokes that nobody could understand the real words, so the parody follows the charts into a different kind of rock and makes fun of the original's sound as much as its words. Cobain approved it, as Yankovic describes it.

The last stop is the one where the method broke, and the map's clearest case of two sides telling different stories. Yankovic says permission came through Coolio's record label. Coolio said nobody asked him personally, and he was unhappy about 'Amish Paradise'. Both accounts are on this stop, and because they conflict, the connection is held at consensus rather than documented.

outro: Five records, twelve years, and one big argument at the end. Read together, the stops show what everyone knew: a parody was only worth making of a song the audience already had in their heads. Jackson, Madonna and Cobain approved, as the stops describe it, and Coolio's account differs from Yankovic's, and the thread leaves both standing. Each artist here leads somewhere else on the map too: open Michael Jackson, the Rolling Stones or Nirvana and follow their other lines out.
